items.title: Unpredictable Intelligence Still Requires Authorization
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become more capable, their behavior may become increasingly difficult to predict. This article examines whether behavioral unpredictability necessarily undermines the ability to govern consequential AI actions. It argues that uncertainty about what a system may propose does not, by itself, defeat action-specific pre-execution authorization. The analysis distinguishes three separate properties: predicting a system's behavior, determining whether a proposed action is permitted under applicable policy and authority, and enforcing that determination before execution. It challenges the assumption that assigning a second, equally or more intelligent AI system to supervise the first resolves the governance problem. Collusion, common-mode failures, and recursive supervision raise questions that additional intelligence alone cannot settle. It separates standing eligibility from runtime authorization: a test-then-trust regime releases on a prior assessment and is exactly as vulnerable to concealed capability as its critics say, while action-specific authorization gates each consequential action under the policy in force at execution. And it distinguishes the authorization requirement, which does not change as capability grows, from the deployment-specific evidence that a boundary remains complete and independent, which must remain valid under the capability model actually in scope. The article develops a three-part analytical framework distinguishing evaluation independence, authority independence, and enforcement independence. It explains why independently derived evaluations do not automatically confer permission, why intelligent supervisors may exercise legitimately delegated authority without becoming an alternative execution path, and why consequential release must remain dependent on an independently enforced authorization verdict. The central architectural argument is conditional. Enforceable authorization requires demonstrated coverage of governed effect-bearing execution paths, protection of the enforcement mechanism against unauthorized control, adequate governing inputs, and valid authority. A boundary-emitted ALLOW permits release; DENY and unresolved ABSTAIN prevent execution. A tamper-evident authorization artifact supports independent reconstruction of the verdict, while separate execution-path evidence is needed to establish that release actually depended on that verdict. The article also examines the limits of this approach, including compromised supervisory determinations, defective authorization inputs, improperly established policy authority, unauthorized AI proliferation outside governed environments, and harmful outcomes from legitimately authorized actions. It does not claim that authorization guarantees safe behavior or universal AI containment. Central conclusion: Behavioral unpredictability does not remove the requirement for enforceable permission over consequential actions. Unpredictability is not permission. Scope A doctrine article in the FERZ AI Governance Corpus. Its claims are analytical and conditional; it asserts no implementation-specific capability and describes no FERZ product. items.title: When disclosure rules are not enough: authorial warrant and judgment in ai-supported scholarship
items.abstract: Abstract Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human–model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor’s capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.

items.title: When Should I Trust This? Designing and Evaluating Factuality Indicators for LLM-based Chatbots
items.abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how people seek information, yet communicating AI factuality to laypeople remains challenging. Through a mixed-methods investigation involving interviews (N=8), a survey (N=1,000), and an experiment (N=5,151), we examine how people evaluate AI-generated information for gardening, mathematical, and medical queries, and how factuality indicators (confidence and sources) shape perceptions. Our interviews and survey show people selectively verify AI responses using external and AI-provided evidence, moderated by contextual factors. Although confidence-indicators affected trust and accuracy perceptions, people hold diverse, ambiguous interpretations of AI confidence. Sources were viewed as crucial, yet users raised concerns about source reliability and verification effort. Our experiment showed that confidence and source-based indicators influenced initial perceptions, but effects disappeared once participants learned the response's correctness. Medical queries elicited skepticism regardless of indicator. Findings motivate helping users interpret model confidence and integrating source information into the interface to support calibrated trust in AI-supported information-seeking.

items.abstract: This cross-sectional quantitative research aimed to study the level of motivation and factors associated with participation in professional development training among personnel at Sansai Hospital, Chiang Mai Province. The sample consisted of 200 personnel at Sansai Hospital, selected through stratified random sampling by mission groups. Data were collected using a questionnaire validated for content validity (IOC > 0.8) and reliability (α = 0.75). Data analysis employed descriptive statistics, comparative tests, and binary logistic regression analysis. Results showed that personnel had an overall high level of motivation (x̄ = 3.95, SD = 0.84), with intrinsic motivation higher than extrinsic motivation (x̄ = 4.21 and 3.68, respectively). Factors significantly associated with training participation decision (p < 0.05) included: self-development (adjusted OR = 2.321, 95% CI = 1.325-4.066), nursing mission group (adjusted OR = 2.440, 95% CI = 1.188-5.012), organizational support (adjusted OR = 2.125, 95% CI = 1.185-3.810), commitment and work inspiration (adjusted OR = 1.874, 95% CI = 1.096-3.204), and years of service (adjusted OR = 0.918, 95% CI = 0.859-0.981). These findings can be applied to develop personnel training policies by emphasizing intrinsic motivation enhancement, increasing organizational support, and reducing barriers to training participation.

items.title: “I Don’t Trust It, but I Have to Trust It”: Trust vs. Use of Online Technology Across the Mental Health Spectrum in the UK
items.abstract: Use of internet-based technologies (IBTs) and artificial intelligence (AI) via eHealth could enhance mental healthcare delivery and accessibility. However, ethical concerns, perceptions of AI capabilities, past experience, and individual differences can influence acceptance and engagement. We qualitatively explored attitudes and behaviours toward IBTs, AI and eHealth, given the overlapping nature of these digital environments, trust, and the possible role of mental health. This exploratory study conducted semi-structured interviews between March and October 2023 with 22 UK-based participants: eight with lived experience of a mental health problem and 14 without. There was no clear difference in participants’ levels of trust in IBTs across mental health status. Participants reported using IBTs despite privacy concerns. Trust was influenced by perceptions of developer trustworthiness, individual traits, and affective responses to IBTs. Convenience, ease of use, and lack of alternatives often outweighed concerns, driving engagement. Our findings highlight that in this group trust is a key factor in IBT and eHealth uptake, but not the sole determinant, highlighting ethical concerns and responsibilities for both UK healthcare providers and developers. There is a need for transparent, ethically grounded, value-sensitive design and implementation of IBTs and AI-enabled eHealth tools that supports genuine user choice, voluntary engagement, and human interaction.

items.title: “What Am I Really Doing with My Own Brain?”: College Students on Learning, Ownership, and AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence gives college students new ways to support their learning, while also raising questions about what they still want to learn and do for themselves. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 undergraduates at a Northeastern liberal arts college to examine how students distinguish between AI use that supports their own thinking and AI use that substitutes for it, what they believe is worth doing on their own, and whether and how purpose enters their reasoning about learning and AI use. Using the Framework Method with a cross-case matrix to compare patterns across participants and topics, we found that students repeatedly drew a line between using AI as a supportive tool and letting it take the place of their own thinking or authorship. Students most often talked about wanting to keep developing their own skills, thinking independently, and knowing what they could actually do without AI. They also wanted the work to still feel “like theirs,” citing ownership, pride, authenticity, and ethical concerns. Students also described pressures that made AI appealing, including heavy workloads, deadlines, grades, convenience, and concerns about falling behind their peers. Although few participants explicitly connected their AI choices to a stated purpose, many described concerns that may be relevant to purpose development, including developing valued skills and strengths, acting on personal values, and becoming the kind of person they hoped to be. We consider these concerns through a purpose-mindset framework while distinguishing our interpretation from participants’ own explanations of their AI choices. The findings suggest that understanding students’ AI use requires attention to what they believe they need to learn and do for themselves.

items.title: A Human–AI Orchestration Framework for Mathematics Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing personalized and adaptive education. Existing research has examined Human–AI hybrid adaptivity and coordination between human participants and AI systems, but clearer conceptualization is needed of the pedagogical coordination of functionally different forms of instructional support, particularly in highly abstract domains such as mathematics. This study proposes a Human–AI Orchestration Framework integrating Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs), Generative AI, and direct teacher support while retaining pedagogical orchestration and responsibility with the teacher. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, the Framework proposes Cognitive Load Redistribution as a theoretical proposition and introduces coordination mechanisms, including Handover Points and a Meta-Prompt. Its practical implementation was explored through an exploratory design pilot with 32 Grade 8 students in an authentic classroom, using observations and feedback to iteratively refine its configuration. The pilot informed several design refinements, including refinement of the Meta-Prompt, introduction of “Call the Teacher,” and adaptation of interaction formats. These formative observations provide preliminary indications of the practical feasibility of coordinating functionally different and potentially complementary forms of instructional support, while the Framework’s educational effectiveness and proposed conceptual mechanisms remain to be systematically evaluated in future research.

items.title: A Right to Delegate to AI: The Regulatory Safety Halo and the Acceleration of Agentic Consumer Markets
items.abstract: Abstract The European Law Institute’s Guiding Principles and Model Rules on Digital Assistants for Consumer Contracts (DACC) propose a right for consumers to use digital assistants in business-to-consumer relations. The DACC’s definition encompasses consumer AI agents (CAIAs), which use AI-generated outputs to determine transactionally relevant matters left open by consumers and initiate or perform transactional actions. The article examines two concerns. First, recognition and safeguards may create a regulatory safety halo, causing consumers to overestimate CAIAs’ technical reliability and the effectiveness of remedies for unwanted outcomes. Second, recognition may accelerate agentic markets, disproportionately benefit incumbents in adjacent digital markets, and foster concentration, to which the DMA and EU competition law provide only partial responses. Legislation should therefore first establish essential rules governing delegation, responsibility and market contestability. Technical implementation may be entrusted to European standardisation bodies, but the Commission’s request should define tasks precisely and maximise transparency and balanced stakeholder participation to mitigate legitimacy concerns. Only once CAIAs are sufficiently reliable and the legal framework more mature should the right to use a CAIA be recognised.

items.title: A Socio-Technical Analysis of AI-Driven Legacy System Modernization in the Public Sector
items.abstract: Purpose: This paper examines the socio-technical limitations of using artificial intelligence (AI) to modernize legacy information systems in the public sector, where continuity of services, policy obligations, security, and public accountability shape technology decisions. Design/methodology/approach: The paper combines a review of literature on public-sector AI adoption and legacy-system modernization with an anonymous survey of more than 50 public-sector technology professionals. Participants represented technical, analytical, management, application-support, and project roles and a range of professional experience. Survey topics included AI benefits and risks, organizational readiness, security and privacy, governance, workforce challenges, and human oversight. Findings: Respondents recognized AI's potential to support modernization but raised concerns about citizen-data protection, compliance, trust in generated outputs, integration, workforce readiness, and accountability. The findings suggest that AI should augment, not replace, experienced professionals and established engineering controls. Survey responses also point to the importance of governance, training, secure environments, phased implementation, and human validation. Originality: The paper brings technical, organizational, institutional, and ethical constraints together in a public-sector legacy-modernization context. It emphasizes that AI should augment, rather than replace, accountable human expertise and that successful adoption depends on governance, secure data practices, validation, and organizational readiness. Research limitations/implications: The survey reflects the views of its participants and should not be treated as representative of all public-sector technology professionals. Environmental impacts were not directly measured in the structured survey. Further research could test these findings across agencies and modernization projects.

items.title: A Survey of Explainable Reinforcement Learning: Targets, Methods and Needs
items.abstract: The success of recent Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has been accompanied by the opacity of their internal mechanisms, due notably to the use of deep neural networks. In order to understand these internal mechanisms and explain the output of these AI models, a set of methods have been proposed, grouped under the domain of eXplainable AI (XAI). This paper focuses on a sub-domain of XAI, called eXplainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL), which aims to explain the actions of an agent that has learned by reinforcement learning. We propose an intuitive taxonomy based on two questions ‘What’ and ‘How’. The first question focuses on the target that the method explains, while the second relates to the way the explanation is provided. We use this taxonomy to provide a state-of-the-art review of over 250 papers. In addition, we present a set of domains close to XRL, which we believe should get attention from the community. Finally, we identify some needs for the field of XRL.

items.title: A systematic literature review of generative AI support for pre-service teachers in designing computational thinking instruction
items.abstract: Abstract Computational Thinking (CT) is increasingly expected across curricula, yet pre-service teachers often report limited preparation for translating CT concepts into instructional practice. This systematic literature review examines how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) supports pre-service teachers’ instructional design and what the available evidence implies for CT-oriented teaching. Using the PRISMA approach, the review synthesised 26 empirical studies identified through Scopus and ScienceDirect under the original eligibility criteria. The evidence base was heterogeneous: only two studies were coded as explicitly addressing CT integration, fifteen as implicitly CT-aligned, and nine as having no identifiable CT integration. Accordingly, indirect studies are treated as contextual evidence rather than direct evidence of CT instructional design. Across the literature, GenAI was used for ideation, lesson planning, feedback, multimedia generation, and iterative refinement. Several studies reported gains or positive experiences in efficiency, confidence, engagement, creativity, or instructional design competence; however, these outcomes were study-specific and should not be generalised as improvements in CT competence. Several studies have linked more productive use of GenAI to human evaluation, AI literacy, pedagogical or subject-matter knowledge, and structured frameworks or training. Reported risks included inaccurate or inconsistent outputs, hallucinations, overreliance, metacognitive laziness, and ethical concerns. Because the search was limited to Scopus and ScienceDirect and applied an open-access criterion, the review may be affected by database and accessibility bias. Overall, direct evidence that GenAI improves CT-specific instructional design remains preliminary; the broader literature more strongly supports a conditional role for GenAI as a pedagogical scaffold in CT-relevant instructional design.

items.title: ABRA: Agent-Bound UI for Human-Agent Communication beyond Chat with Reusable Views
items.abstract: Agents can create rich representations, yet these representations are rarely used as a medium for expressing user intent. We present Agent-Bound UI, an interaction model that separates reusable interaction structures from task-specific meanings. Agents bind task-specific meanings to interactions in reusable views and publish the resulting bindings as shared state, enabling humans and agents to understand and act on shared surfaces whose meanings vary across tasks. We implement ABRA, a framework-agnostic prototype of Agent-Bound UI, in which users and agents collaborate through chat and shared interactive canvases. We demonstrate ABRA through a representative use case and evaluate four LLM-backed agents on canvas authoring, owner-side consequence resolution, and cross-agent invocation. The code and demo video are available at https://github.com/megagonlabs/abra.

items.title: Abstract Priorities, Concrete Rewards: How Stated Preferences Relate to What People Reward in AI Responses
items.abstract: AI assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are trained on human feedback and increasingly personalized to users' stated preferences. Yet how closely these preferences reflect what people reward in responses remains unclear. We compare stated and revealed preferences in the public PRISM dataset, in which 1,396 participants reported how much seven response attributes mattered to them and then rated 29,347 responses from 21 LLMs. Among responses to the same prompt, features the survey never asked about, such as response length, formatting and refusal language, were at least as strongly associated with ratings as text proxies of the surveyed attributes. Whether stated priorities matched ratings depended on how attributes were measured: participants who prioritized an attribute favoured responses from models that others perceived as strong on it, but not responses that scored higher on text proxies for it. Written feedback was more telling: participants who asked for shorter answers, even in earlier conversations, gave length less weight in their ratings, and those asking for longer answers gave it more. Their relative priorities over the surveyed attributes, however, did not predict this weight. Reasons given for choices reflected perceived attributes more than measured features. Participants also differed stably in how much they weighted several concrete features, especially length, but with a median of 6 conversations per participant, these weights were estimated poorly. The largest gain from personal information in predicting held-out choices was 0.13 percentage points, compared with 1.11 for a stronger pooled model. Stated priorities thus track perceived attributes of AI responses but say little about the concrete features that ratings reward, a distinction that matters for preference elicitation and AI personalization.

items.title: Adaptive Performance as a Pathway to Human Capital Readiness: The Roles of Digital Readiness and Organizational Resilience
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how learning agility and change self-efficacy are associated with human capital readiness through adaptive performance and whether digital readiness and organizational resilience condition these relationships. Using a quantitative explanatory design, cross-sectional survey data from 350 professional workers across government, state-owned enterprises, banking, higher education, and digital-based private organizations in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, were analyzed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Learning agility (β = 0.186, p = 0.004) and change self-efficacy (β = 0.301, p < 0.001) were positively associated with adaptive performance, while adaptive performance was positively associated with human capital readiness (β = 0.498, p < 0.001). The model explained 74.6% of the variance in adaptive performance and 73.4% in human capital readiness. Digital readiness did not significantly moderate either capability-performance relationship. Organizational resilience strengthened the learning agility-adaptive performance relationship (β = 0.135, p = 0.010) but weakened the change self-efficacy-adaptive performance relationship (β = -0.196, p = 0.016). These findings position adaptive performance as a central behavioral pathway through which individual capabilities relate to workforce readiness and show that organizational context operates asymmetrically rather than uniformly. Organizations should pair digital investment with learning-oriented work design, confidence-building support, managerial flexibility, and knowledge-sharing mechanisms. items.title: Adoption and Impacts of a Socratic Generative AI Tutor in Undergraduate Algebra
items.abstract: Instructors looking to support personalized mathematics learning may provide access to generative AI tutoring tools. Few studies explore the effectiveness of these systems in classroom settings. This is particularly important in mathematics, where genAI is a shift from historic adaptive intelligent tutoring systems. We evaluated undergraduate algebra students’ (n=58) use of the Socratic generative AI tutor, Khanmigo, through a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study using survey, registrar, grades, and software usage data. One course section was assigned four Khanmigo activities throughout the semester (experimental), while the other was provided access and an introductory activity only (control). A Wilcoxon Rank Sum test showed that experimental students engaged in significantly more chats than control students (p<0.05), controlling for in-class activities. Instrumental help seeking was positively correlated with Khanmigo use, while intentions of seeking help from technology sources were negatively correlated with use. Khanmigo use did significantly predict mathematics grades after controlling for prior GPA and course section. Most students reported using Khanmigo for homework help and exam prep, though lack of visuals and the Socratic design limited perceived usefulness for some students. Integrating genAI tutoring systems into class activities and setting student expectations may improve the likelihood of students using them effectively for learning.

items.title: Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization
items.abstract: LLM agents can evolve by learning from accumulated experience. Existing approaches extract reusable external knowledge, such as skills and memories, from experience to guide subsequent task solving, with some further internalizing this knowledge through model training. However, different ways of analyzing and transforming the same experience can yield knowledge with substantially different utility, even when the resulting guidance appears reasonable. Inspired by consistency regularization, we identify consistent utility gains across different ways of analyzing the same experience, rather than relying on any single way of analyzing it. We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized knowledge-model co-evolution. It constructs evolution views by perturbing how the same experience is analyzed, producing different knowledge candidates. Knowledge updates are then guided by common gain, which accounts for utility gains and their consistency across views. During model evolution, self-distillation internalizes the evolved knowledge alongside reinforcement learning, using knowledge associated with consistent utility degradation as a contrastive reference. The two processes interleave, with model updates driving further knowledge evolution. Experiments across diverse domains show that SPLICE outperforms knowledge evolution and model training baselines by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points in average accuracy, while its evolved knowledge reduces output tokens per correct solution by up to 44% and transfers across model sizes and families.

items.title: AI awareness and work stress among university teachers: The moderating roles of digital literacy and perceived organizational support
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) gradually enters the teaching and research contexts of higher education institutions, university teachers’ different perceptions of AI may elicit different psychological responses. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources model, this study examines the effects of AI Challenge Awareness and AI Threat Awareness on university teachers’ Work Stress, and further analyzes the moderating roles of Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support. Using university teachers as the research subjects, 421 valid samples were obtained through a questionnaire survey, and hierarchical regression analysis was employed to test the research hypotheses. The results indicate that AI Challenge Awareness is significantly and negatively correlated with university teachers’ Work Stress, whereas AI Threat Awareness is significantly and positively correlated with Work Stress. Both Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support significantly weaken the positive effect of AI Threat Awareness on Work Stress, but neither of their moderating effects on the relationship between AI Challenge Awareness and Work Stress reaches a significant level. The findings suggest that university teachers’ perceptions of AI do not merely manifest as a source of stress; rather, their effects depend on individuals’ different interpretations of the work-related changes brought about by AI. Compared with challenge-oriented perceptions, threat-oriented perceptions are more readily transformed into Work Stress, while Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support can, to a certain extent, buffer the stress induced by threat-oriented perceptions. The conclusions of this study help to deepen the understanding of individual differences in university teachers’ psychological responses in the context of AI, and provide references for higher education institutions to optimize the AI application environment and improve teacher support measures.

items.abstract: Abstract: Factchecking is among the key mechanisms for addressing information disorder. In the context of the growing integration of artificial intelligence, particularly large language models, into the information environment, the need for reliable information is increasing while access to it is more challenging. Thus, generative artificial intelligence can be both – an asset and a risk to factcheckers. The present study aims to examine the extent to which Claude.ai and ChatGPT can factcheck claims in Bulgarian. The experiment was conducted using a free skill developed by Nauka.bg. The claims were selected from the “Verified” section of Factcheck.bg, the largest fact-checking platform in Bulgaria. Through comparative content analysis, the study found that in most cases both models correctly identify false claims in accordance with Factcheck.bg’s publications. Claude.ai demonstrates a more authoritative tone and provides concise explanations supporting its verdicts. ChatGPT is more hesitant but offers greater detail, precision, and clarity in its explanations. Notably, ChatGPT rarely references its sources, whereas Claude.ai occasionally links to unreliable sources. A positive trend is Claude.ai’s note to consult official factchecking organizations and verified information sources.The results confirm the hypothesis that artificial intelligence can assist factcheckers but cannot replace human expertise in the verification process. Keywords: disinformation, factchecking, artificial intelligence, large language models, ChatGPT, Claude.ai.

items.title: AI Governance and the Architecture of Dependency
items.abstract: A system does not have to remove choice in order to shape it. It can define the problem, structure the options that appear, and create conditions under which a voluntary choice becomes costly to reverse. These mechanisms predate artificial intelligence. This paper asks what changes when AI-mediated systems operate them at greater speed, scale, and adaptability, and when the people subject to them cannot practically inspect, contest, or leave. The paper develops a four-part lens (problem definition, choice architecture, dependency formation, reversibility) and distinguishes institutional dependency from epistemic dependency. It adds an agency and accountability audit of six questions: who sets the objective, who controls the data, model and infrastructure, who can inspect the evidence, who bears the cost of error, who can override or replace the system, and what alternatives remain. Its central hypothesis, an accountability asymmetry, is stated with the evidence that would weaken it. A rubric scores safeguards by whether they have been exercised, not merely documented, and is applied to three current arrangements: the Robodebt scheme, the Medicare WISeR model, and the UnitedHealth nH Predict litigation. Where public evidence allows no score, the gap is reported as a finding. Appendices provide a one-page citizen audit card and a legal and case status snapshot as of 21 October 2026. This is a working paper. It has not been peer reviewed and is not legal advice. Claims are labelled documented, reported, interpretation, or hypothesis. The rubric is unvalidated and was scored by a single rater from public sources. Companion to Johnson (2026a) and Johnson (2026b).

items.title: AI literacy is directly associated with positive attitudes and indirectly associated with negative attitudes through AI anxiety: a cross-sectional study of preservice teachers
items.abstract: Introduction Positive and negative attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) may have partly distinct psychological correlates. This cross-sectional study examined whether AI anxiety statistically accounted for associations between AI literacy and positive and negative attitudes toward AI among preservice teachers. Methods Participants were 335 preservice teachers enrolled in a faculty of education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale, and a personal information form. Two indirect-effect models were estimated using PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for prior AI training. Results AI literacy was negatively associated with AI anxiety and positively associated with positive attitudes toward AI. AI anxiety was positively associated with negative attitudes but was not significantly associated with positive attitudes. The indirect association through AI anxiety was significant for negative attitudes but not for positive attitudes, and a direct bootstrap contrast confirmed that the two indirect effects differed significantly (B = −0.118, 95% CI [−0.201, −0.039]). Prior AI training was not significantly associated with either attitude dimension. A sensitivity analysis excluding the three reverse-worded AI literacy items reproduced this pattern. Discussion The findings indicate that positive and negative attitudes toward AI may have partly distinct psychological correlates: AI literacy is directly related to positive evaluations, whereas its association with negative evaluations is statistically linked to AI anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional, the indirect effects should not be interpreted as evidence of causal mediation.

items.title: AI-Augmented Business Training and Development for Organizational Sustainability
items.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be integrated into business training and development (T&D) to strengthen organizational capacity for long-term viability. Drawing on action learning, experiential learning, and enterprise education, it outlines how AI-enabled tools, such as intelligent coaching systems, adaptive feedback mechanisms, and decision-support platforms, can support the development of transversal capabilities, including systemic thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making. The analysis adopts a design perspective, advancing an architecture for AI-augmented training that connects educational and workplace contexts. Strategic considerations are proposed for creating individualized and scalable learning environments that address the dual imperative of workforce development and organizational adaptability under complex, evolving conditions. The chapter integrates pedagogical models and systems design principles to offer a coherent framework for embedding AI in organizational T&D.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a nascent technology that could become a general-purpose technology and can have significant impacts on economic development, productivity growth, labour markets and good governance. The study will delve into the potential impact of Artificial Intelligence on the economy and job landscape of India as part of the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047. The study uses qualitative review-based research methodology that is based on analyzing evidence from the academic literature, government documents, as well as reports produced by national and international institutions. AI has the potential to augment productivity, innovate solutions, modernize industries, contribute to digital governance and create job opportunities, as revealed by this study. At the same time, the implementation of AI can be challenging due to the changes in labor markets, lack of skills, digital divide, fragility of the informal sector, data privacy and security concerns, algorithmic biases, and institutional preparedness. In this study, it is argued that AI will not necessarily take the place of jobs, but rather change the employment type if suitable reskilling measures are taken. It identifies the following policy priorities – human capital, digital infrastructure, responsible AI governance, research and innovation, and social protection.

items.abstract: Accelerated progress in digital technologies has influenced all industries. Interest in embracing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education and research is flourishing among scholars, practitioners, educators, students, and the general public. Educational institutions now need to transform their traditional approach towards teaching and research by implementing innovative technologies. However, controversies surrounding the use of AI in education or research require deeper examination. Moreover, integration sustainability in business education has become an obligation for universities around the world. The significance of universities in empowering generations to tackle complex sustainability issues calls for ground-breaking solutions. In this regard, AI with its immense capabilities can offer a unique approach. This chapter aims to explore AI trends and tendencies in teaching and research and to shed light on the role of AI in sustainability education. The main research question is: How can AI be incorporated into teaching to enhance sustainability education? To achieve research aims, the qualitative research method was used and expert interview approach was applied. This research contributes to the discussion of introducing AI in sustainability education and research agenda by delving into the multifaceted intersection of AI, sustainability and education. Based on the results, a theoretical framework is proposed to adopt AI into sustainable development teaching. The findings benefit academics, educators, researchers, policymakers and industry representatives to grasp future trends in sustainability education through AI-powered initiatives.

items.title: AI-Enabled School Management for Sustainable Education: A Systematic Review of Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: This review examines the various ways artificial intelligence (AI) can influence school management and its potential to promote sustainable education. It brings together the findings from earlier studies to illustrate how schools are using AI to simplify administrative tasks, enrich learning experiences, and support sustainable education efforts. Key uses include AI tools for real-time data analysis, better resource management, and personalised learning paths that connect students with real-world environmental issues. By managing tasks such as data cleaning and report generation, AI enables educators and staff to dedicate more time to strategic initiatives like developing curricula and engaging the community in sustainability projects. The review also highlights major challenges and risks of using AI in education, such as concerns about data privacy, the need for reliable infrastructure, and ethical issues related to algorithmic bias. The findings show that although AI provides powerful tools for creating efficient and environmentally conscious schools, successful and fair implementation requires careful planning, targeted teacher training, and a focus on equal access. The article concludes by emphasising key areas for future research, underlining the need for robust frameworks to enable schools to use AI responsibly while promoting both academic excellence and a culture of sustainability and sustainable education.

items.title: AI-Guided Reflection to Bridge Formal Learning and Work
items.abstract: Formal on-demand online courses offer professionals a structured way to acquire knowledge that is relevant to their work, and can complement workplace learning. However, connecting between such formal learning and work brings two essential challenges: (1) identifying and articulating work-grounded learning objectives and mapping them to formal learning; and (2) transferring knowledge newly acquired in the learning space to the workplace. Reflection, guided by AI tools, may be a useful way to support these processes. This chapter first frames reflective practice as a way of working—with continuous reflection alongside work—and then presents three cases where AI-guided reflection bridged formal learning and work. In a socio-technical design space, AI tools can prompt and structure reflection, provide feedback, and offer data analytics as a “looking glass” on work practice. In doing so, they steer attention and shape how professionals reflect. At the same time, professionals retain agency to choose, configure, and use tools; but professionals’ competence is a pre-requisite for effective such reflective practice. Subsequently, our vision for technology-oriented research is to further develop systems that (1) facilitate the articulation of learning needs, (2) facilitate knowledge transfer by using rich and multimodal evidence from the workplace to support AI-guided reflection, and (3) expand interaction affordances towards more situated and embodied AI-guidance (e.g., multimodal sensing and analytics, ambient prompts, voice-first coaching, agentic companions) that may better fit workplace constraints and ways of working, and (4) help professionals further develop their agency in reflective practice through such hybrid, multimodal and embodied AI. In parallel, a challenge for workplace learning-oriented research is to examine AI-guidance in-situ and to develop socio-technical AI design patterns, as combinations of technology design and usage. Formal on-demand learning providers are uniquely positioned to take up such AI-guidance as part of their offerings, with a recommendation to provide both tools and training in using tools, and teaching, coaching, and mentoring to build professionals’ reflection competence.

items.title: ALGORITHMIC WILDERNESS: AI LITERACY, TECHNOLOGICAL MEDIATION, AND DECISION-MAKING AMONG GENERATION Z HIKERS
items.abstract: This phenomenological study explores the lived experiences of Thai Generation Z hikers, thoroughly examining the critical intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and complex decision-making in wilderness environments. As young adventurers increasingly pursue nature-based eco-experientia for psychological restoration, AI has rapidly evolved into an active, front-facing backcountry companion. Using the Theory of Technological Mediation alongside robust methodological triangulation—including in-depth interviews, focus groups, and interactive discussions with university-aged hikers—this research examines how algorithmic tools profoundly reshape human-nature relationships. The empirical findings clearly show that AI is seamlessly integrated throughout the trekking lifecycle, functioning as a vital digital safety net that mitigates environmental uncertainty. However, this deep integration precipitates a highly complex socio-technical paradox. While participants consistently exhibit exceptional functional AI literacy, an emerging algorithmic dependency actively threatens to erode traditional, intuitive wilderness judgment. Ultimately, AI facilitates a hermeneutic relationship in which pristine nature is interpreted through curated data, fundamentally transforming raw exploration into a mediated digital reality that urgently requires careful preservation of human agency within adventure tourism.

items.title: An Old Answer to a New Problem: The Degree-Free Model for Higher Education in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Generative AI has not created the governance crisis in higher education credentialing; it has made it harder to ignore. The academic degree is higher education’s principal instrument for governing access to occupations. Its signaling value depends on assessed work reflecting individual competence. AI weakens that link: in blind marking, AI-written exam answers went largely undetected and, on average, outscored students, while detection tools trail each new model. Strengthening surveillance restores procedural control only at the cost of assessment validity. Drawing on credentialism and signaling theory, this paper argues that the response may need to include institutional redesign, not only pedagogical adjustment. It proposes a degree-free model, illustrated by the yeshiva: a centuries-old institution organized around formation, community, and recognized mastery rather than certification. Labor markets already partly follow this logic, as employers substitute direct observation of performance for the degree within three to five years of hire. Three recommendations follow. Outside safety-critical fields, institutions could stop issuing degrees while continuing to teach. Public investment should shift from surveillance-based assessment toward authentic evaluation. Reform should be differentiated by field, retaining mandatory credentialing in licensed and safety-critical professions. The model is offered as a proposition for debate, not a blueprint.

items.title: Ancestors in the machine: personhood, spirituality, and artificial intelligence - AI ethics in African cosmology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping human agency, knowledge production, decision-making, and social relations, raising ethical questions about personhood, responsibility, and technological governance. Although existing scholarship addresses relational personhood, Ubuntu, decolonial AI, indigenous knowledge, data justice, and responsible innovation, ancestral ontology and cultural memory remain comparatively underexplored in AI ethics. This study examines how African, particularly Igbo, cosmological understandings of personhood, relationality, spirituality, community, and ancestral continuity can inform ethical AI development and governance. It aims to develop an Ancestral-Relational AI Ethics Framework (AR-AIEF) that integrates African philosophical insights into contemporary debates on technological personhood and accountability. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, non-empirical philosophical design combining conceptual analysis, hermeneutical interpretation, and a critical interdisciplinary review of relevant philosophical, theological, cultural, and AI ethics literature. As a conceptual inquiry, it involves no human participants or statistical sampling. The analysis identifies relational personhood, distributed responsibility, ancestral continuity, intergenerational accountability, communal justice, and human flourishing as key principles for an African-informed approach to AI ethics. It does not equate AI systems with ancestors or attribute spirituality to machines; rather, ancestral relationality provides a lens for examining how AI stores, reproduces, simulates, and mediates cultural memory and human identity. The study contributes an African cosmological perspective to global AI ethics and recommends culturally plural governance, indigenous epistemic participation, protection of ancestral knowledge, meaningful human accountability, and intergenerationally responsible innovation. It argues that ethical AI must consider not only technological capabilities but also the communal relationships and human futures those capabilities shape.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the 2027 Elections: Comparing Urban and Rural Voters' Responses to AI-Generated Campaign Messages in Abia State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering Nigerian electoral communication ahead of the 2027 general elections, raising concerns about authenticity, trust and misinformation. This exploratory study examined how voters aged 18–40 in Abia State, Nigeria, understand, feel about and respond to AI-generated and AI-assisted campaign messages, and how urban/semi-urban and rural voters compare. Method: A qualitative exploratory design was adopted. Twenty voters (ten urban/semi-urban and ten rural) were purposively selected from communities across Abia State and interviewed individually using six AI-generated or AI-assisted campaign materials (CM1–CM6), supplemented by observation notes. Data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and interpreted with the Elaboration Likelihood Model. Findings: AI familiarity varied within both groups rather than simply between them. Participants separated emotional appeal from credibility, and realistic fabrication caused more concern than obvious satire. The messages stimulated attention, discussion and verification more readily than candidate support, and rural participants relied more on interpersonal and community verification networks. Conclusion: Within this sample, AI-generated campaign messages shaped electoral judgement through credibility, emotional appeal, realism and verification conditions rather than automatic vote conversion. As exploratory findings, these are not statistically generalisable but offer propositions for larger studies.

items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and nurses’ turnover intention during healthcare digital transformation: the mediating role of occupational fatigue
items.abstract: Background The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare is associated with new psychological challenges. However, the extent of its impact on nursing workforce stability is unclear. Aim To explore the relationship between AI anxiety and turnover intention of clinical nurses, and the mediating effect of occupational fatigue and the moderating effect of emotional intelligence (EI). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to June 2026 among 404 clinical nurses from four hospitals in Jiangsu Province, China. Data were collected using the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS), Health Workers’ Occupational Fatigue Scale (HWOFS), Turnover Intention Scale (TIS) and Wong and Law Emotional Intelligence Scale (WLEIS). Mediation was tested using structural equation modelling with bootstrap resampling, while moderation was tested using moderated regression analysis. Results Differences in baseline turnover intentions across age, department, and professional title level were statistically significant (all p < 0.001). Path analysis showed that AI anxiety was positively associated with occupational fatigue (β = 0.611, p < 0.001) and turnover intention (β = 0.530, p < 0.001). Occupational fatigue partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and turnover intention (indirect effect = 0.299, 95% CI: 0.129, 0.379). EI had a significant negative main effect on occupational fatigue (b = −0.257, p < 0.001), but it did not significantly moderate the association between AI anxiety and occupational fatigue. Conclusion AI anxiety is significantly correlated with the turnover intention of clinical nurses, and occupational fatigue may represent a potential pathway linking AI anxiety and turnover intention. Although EI is associated with lower levels of occupational fatigue, it fails to cushion the impact of AI anxiety, a specific stressor. Hospital administrators should focus on targeted AI literacy improvement plans and specific fatigue relief strategies to retain clinical nursing staff.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ECONOMIC SECURITY: EMERGING RISKS, GOVERNANCE CHALLENGES, AND RESILIENCE STRATEGIES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a general-purpose technology with significant implications for economic growth, employment, financial stability, and national security. This article examines how AI reshapes economic security, understood as the capacity of households, firms, and states to withstand shocks to income, markets, and critical infrastructure. Using a structured narrative review of academic research, international policy reports, regulatory frameworks, and technical safety studies, the article identifies four principal risk domains: labor-market disruption, market concentration and infrastructure dependence, financial instability, and malicious or geopolitical misuse. The review also examines governance challenges arising from fragmented regulatory approaches, limited institutional capacity, incomplete evidence, and the rapid pace of technological deployment. The findings indicate that AI-related risks are interconnected and that vulnerabilities can spread through shared models, concentrated computing infrastructure, and correlated institutional decisions. In response, the article proposes a layered resilience framework combining adaptive regulation, competition policy, financial supervision, workforce investment, and international coordination. It concludes that economic security depends not only on preventing harmful applications of AI but also on strengthening institutions’ ability to anticipate, absorb, and recover from technological shocks.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Robotics: The Future of Humanity, Mass Unemployment, Hunger, and the Global Economic Crisis
items.abstract: Abstract This working paper examines the potential economic and social consequences of accelerating artificial intelligence, robotics, and large-scale automation, with particular attention to technological unemployment, income insecurity, wealth concentration, declining purchasing power, food insecurity, and social instability. It addresses a fundamental question: What happens when machines can produce an increasing share of the goods and services humanity needs, while large numbers of people lose the employment income required to purchase those goods and services? The paper explores how automation may transform employment across agriculture, manufacturing, construction, transportation, commerce, professional services, and knowledge-based occupations. It considers the possibility that productivity gains may become increasingly concentrated among the owners of advanced technologies, while affected workers and households experience economic insecurity. Particular attention is given to developing and low-income countries, where limited household savings, informal employment, weak social protection systems, and restricted public resources may amplify the consequences of rapid technological displacement. Rather than assuming that mass unemployment, hunger, or social unrest are inevitable, the paper presents alternative future scenarios for 2036–2045 and identifies economic, institutional, and social conditions that could increase or reduce these risks. It proposes a preventive policy framework incorporating international open vocational transition institutes, proactive workforce reskilling, social funds supported by productivity and capital returns, income protection mechanisms, food security safeguards, economic early-warning indicators, and contingency plans for large-scale employment disruption. The paper calls upon researchers, governments, universities, international organizations, labor institutions, and technology companies to investigate these risks before technological displacement exceeds the capacity of societies to adapt. The central concern is not whether machines will become more productive than human beings, but whether humanity can develop economic and social institutions that ensure the benefits of technological progress remain accessible to all. This publication is an exploratory working paper and public policy proposal. It does not claim to establish a new technological discovery, present a validated economic model, or demonstrate that widespread unemployment or social crises are inevitable. items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Smart Mobility Nexus: A Systematic Evidence Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping transportation through predictive analytics, intelligent infrastructure, connected mobility, autonomous systems and energy-responsive transport management. This systematic evidence review examines the AI-smart mobility nexus with an emphasis on intelligent transportation infrastructure and operational sustainability. Following PRISMA 2020, 30 eligible sources published between 2015 and 2026 were synthesised from Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar. The corpus comprised 29 review, survey, meta-review, bibliometric or conceptual syntheses and one case study; accordingly, evidence was interpreted qualitatively and no pooled effect estimates were calculated. Five dominant domains emerged: AI-enabled traffic management, connected transportation infrastructure, safety and risk reduction, electric and renewable-energy-integrated mobility, and operational sustainability. Across the included literature, AI was generally associated with improved prediction, routing, incident recognition, system coordination, infrastructure monitoring and energy-management capability, although transferability depended on data quality, connectivity, infrastructure readiness, grid capacity and institutional capability. Operational efficiency did not consistently imply broader environmental or social sustainability. Interpreted through Technological Innovation Systems and Sustainability Transition perspectives, the evidence suggests that sustainable smart mobility depends on coordinated technological, infrastructural, institutional and energy-system development. The review therefore supports a qualified conclusion: AI can contribute to safer and more efficient mobility, but stronger primary, longitudinal and geographically diverse evidence is needed to establish durable environmental and social outcomes.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Emergency Department Triage and Risk Stratification: A Review
items.abstract: Researchers increasingly investigate artificial intelligence (AI) as a tool to support triage and early risk stratification in emergency departments. However, improved predictive performance does not necessarily translate into safer decisions or better patient outcomes. This critical narrative review examines the evidence for AI in adult ED care, with particular emphasis on prospective evaluation, patient safety, and clinical implementation. The review compares conventional triage systems, early warning scores, and clinician assessment with machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models. It examines commonly used data inputs, prediction timing, model discrimination, calibration, external validation, and the limitations of outcome definitions. Attention is given to the distinction between predicting clinical deterioration, critical care need, short-term mortality, and hospital admission. Evidence is considered across retrospective development, external validation, silent prospective evaluation, clinician-visible implementation, and randomized trials. AI may help identify patients requiring closer assessment by integrating information from multiple sources. Nevertheless, its clinical value depends on data quality, timely predictions, generalizability, and healthcare professionals' ability to interpret outputs appropriately. Important risks include under-triage, automation bias, unequal performance across patient groups, and increased clinical workload. Prospective studies and randomized trials are therefore essential to establish whether AI-supported decisions improve patient outcomes compared with usual care. Future research should prioritize multicenter clinical evaluations, consistent outcome reporting, subgroup assessment, and continuous monitoring after deployment. AI implementation should also include clear accountability, human oversight, and procedures for reviewing adverse events. Evidence of predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to justify routine adoption. Clinical integration should depend on demonstrated safety and meaningful benefit for patients.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges
items.abstract: Introduction Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Agricultural Teaching, Research, and Skill Development for Sustainable Development in Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping agricultural education globally, but its integration in Nigeria remains in its early stages. This chapter focuses on systematically embedding AI into Nigeria’s agricultural education through pedagogical innovation, institutional readiness, and skills development. Instead of broadly surveying AI’s role, it critically analyzes the necessary frameworks, practices, and policies for its operational inclusion in agricultural training and research. Drawing from empirical evidence and global models (India, Kenya, Brazil, and China), the chapter explores AI-enhanced pedagogies, such as smart learning environments and digital simulations, to bolster competencies in precision agriculture, climate-smart farming, and agribusiness management. The analysis identifies four key dimensions for AI integration: curriculum redesign for competency-based learning; institutional capacity and infrastructure; ethical governance of digital systems; and alignment with Nigeria’s Digital Economy and AI Strategies. While awareness and pilot initiatives are on the rise, challenges like weak infrastructure, limited staff training, and fragmented policy implementation restrict large-scale adoption. The chapter proposes a phased integration model—encompassing awareness, capacity building, curriculum reform, and adaptive feedback—to facilitate sustainable transformation. Ultimately, it argues that AI should be regarded not just as a technological innovation but as a pedagogical framework vital for transforming Nigeria’s agricultural education ecosystem. By aligning AI with national sustainability goals, Nigeria can develop a new generation of digitally skilled, sustainability-focused agricultural professionals prepared for the challenges of the twenty-first-century food system.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare and human resource management: a review of the global divide, Pakistan's landscape and institutional innovations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare and organizational management worldwide, yet its benefits remain unevenly distributed between high-income and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This review examines the structural drivers of this global AI divide, situates Pakistan's healthcare and digital infrastructure challenges within this context, and presents an institutional case study of four AI-enabled interventions implemented at the Sindh Integrated Emergency and Health Services (SIEHS), an emergency and health services organization under the Health Department, Government of Sindh, Pakistan: an AI-driven recruitment and candidate-job matching system (Talent Match Live), a facial-recognition and geolocation-based field monitoring application, an AI-assisted CCTV training-monitoring system, and an AI-augmented telemedicine triage service embedded within SIEHS's Teletabeeb telehealth department. Each intervention is evaluated against comparable systems documented in the international literature to assess feasibility, evidence of effectiveness, and associated ethical risks. A responsible-adoption framework is proposed to guide organizations in resource-constrained settings toward AI integration that is effective, equitable, and ethically governed. The review concludes that while AI offers meaningful efficiency and access gains for LMIC public-sector organizations such as SIEHS, sustainable adoption requires deliberate attention to data protection, algorithmic bias, workforce consent, and alignment with international ethical guidance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Advancing SDG 4 on Quality Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence implementation in the education field provides revolutionary methods to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4): ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning skills acquisition. This chapter assesses the strategic role of the integration of AI in the enhancement of the quality and efficiency of the post-primary education sectors. Through the adoption of the mixed research method that implies the analysis of the literature reviews and case studies, the study investigates the strategic role of AI technologies towards improved teaching practices and the effectiveness of the institutions. This study reveals the potential strategic role that AI technologies can play in reducing the gap in education access and the effective acquisition and implementation of information-based decisions in post-primary educational sectors. Through the strategic adoption of AI technologies, the study reveals the continued challenges posed by ethical approaches towards the adoption of the technologies and the implementation of equity towards capacity building. This study has proved that the adoption of AI technology in post-primary educational sectors can be an effective strategic mechanism towards the goal of SDG 4. items.title: Artificial intelligence in religious education: teacher perspectives from a national professional development context
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines teachers’ perceptions of and orientations to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the context of Religious Education (RE), drawing on survey data collected from 54 in-service RE teachers participating in the SUB8 professional development programme in Greece. Using a descriptive survey design grounded in the frameworks of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), AI literacy, and digital self-efficacy, the study maps teachers’ reported practices, competencies, and concerns across seven thematic dimensions. Findings indicate generally positive orientations towards AI-assisted instructional design within this cohort, alongside significant theological and pedagogical concerns regarding its use in spiritually sensitive contexts. Qualitative responses point to three recurring themes: the productive utility of AI for lesson preparation and differentiation; persistent concerns about accuracy, depth, and the reliability of AI-generated content; and a strong consensus that AI must function as a supplementary pedagogical tool, subordinate to the relational and experiential dimensions of RE. Because participants were self-selected members of an AI-focused training programme and were surveyed immediately upon its completion, these findings are interpreted as descriptive of this specific professional development context rather than of Greek RE teachers in general. The study complements recent comparative evidence from Germany and Poland by providing, to the author’s knowledge, the first empirical account of AI perceptions among RE teachers within an Orthodox national professional development context, and it foregrounds a theological and epistemological dimension still largely absent from AI-in-education research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Talent Acquisition: An Empirical Assessment of Recruitment Outcomes and Responsible Use
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to source applicants, display screening packages, match candidates, communicate with applicants, and analyse workforce data. Processing speed alone does not indicate whether it is AI-powered. Recruitment outcomes also include shortlist relevance, applicant delight, recruiter productivity, and high-quality decisions. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and five perceived skill-acquisition outcomes, drawing on questionnaire responses from 70 individuals. The analysis uses descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and separate simple linear regression. AI adoption undoubtedly improves recruitment performance (β = 0.546, R2 = 0.282), recruitment effectiveness (β = 0.514, R2 = 0.295), perceived candidate experience (β = 0.569, R2 = 0.363), recruiter productivity (β = 0.498, R2 = 0.329) and overall performance of talent acquisition (β = 0.341, R2 = 0.120). All five regression relationships are statistically significant at the 5% level. Candidate experience has the highest R2 among the five factors, while specific skill acquisition performance has the lowest. Additionally, respondents who report greater AI adoption tend to report more favourable recruiting outcomes, but the study does not establish causality or confirm changes in overall objective hiring performance. The article discusses these findings in relation to fairness, transparency, confidentiality, and human oversight. It recommends that firms assess the use of multiple end-result markers in AI-enabled hiring and conduct meaningful human assessment of the resulting options.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Integration and Its Effectiveness on Higher Vocational Education Management and School–Enterprise Talent Training
items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) integration, management effectiveness, and school–enterprise collaborative talent training at Guangzhou Huali Vocational College of Science and Technology, China. A descriptive-correlational quantitative design involved 159 students and 101 teachers during the second semester of academic year 2025–2026. Students were included through total enumeration and teachers through purposive sampling. A researcher-developed questionnaire was validated by five experts and pilot-tested with 30 individuals; Cronbach’s alpha was 0.96. Analysis used frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t tests, one-way analysis of variance, and Pearson correlations. Both groups rated AI integration as high, management effectiveness to a high extent, and training success to a high degree. Students’ assessments differed significantly by enterprise exposure across all three constructs; teachers’ AI integration assessments differed by position. AI integration correlated positively with management effectiveness for students (r = 0.8839) and teachers (r = 0.9225). Management effectiveness correlated positively with training success for students (r = 0.9399) and teachers (r = 0.9586). The findings support coordinated curriculum, assessment, supervision, faculty development, and workplace learning. A Comprehensive AI Integration Framework was proposed to strengthen institutional practices and collaborative training. The relationships indicate association rather than causation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy and innovative behavior among clinical nurses: the roles of AI self-efficacy and organizational innovation climate
items.abstract: Objective To investigate the current status and related factors of innovative behavior among clinical nurses in tertiary hospitals and explore the relationships and pathways among artificial intelligence literacy, AI self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and nurse innovative behavior, for providing a basis for targeted nursing management strategies. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted on 850 nurses from six tertiary medical institutions using a stratified survey approach in Yueyang city, Hunan province, from June to July 2026, in the General Information Questionnaire, Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, Organizational Innovation Climate Scale, and Nurse Innovative Behavior Scale were used. AMOS 24.0 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis to assess the model fit of the scales. SPSS 26.0 was used for descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. PROCESS macro version 4.2 Models 4 and 14 tested mediation and moderated mediation effects. Results A total of 850 valid questionnaires were obtained, with a valid questionnaire rate of 95.3%. The mean nurse innovative behavior score was 37.93±6.50. The measurement model for the four scales showed good fit, and the scales demonstrated good convergent validity and some evidence of discriminant validity. Artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and innovative behavior showed positive associations with one another (r = 0.609–0.797, P < 0.01). Educational level, professional title, participation in research or innovation activities, artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, and organizational innovation climate were factors associated with nurse innovative behavior and explained 60.9% of the total variance. Artificial intelligence self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between artificial intelligence literacy and nurse innovative behavior. The indirect effect was 0.322, with a 95% CI of 0.243–0.403, accounting for 52.90% of the total effect. Organizational innovation climate moderated the relationship between artificial intelligence self-efficacy and nurse innovative behavior (b = 0.051, P < 0.01). The index of moderated mediation was 0.041, with a 95% CI of 0.009–0.078. Conclusion AI literacy was closely related to nurse innovative behavior, with AI self-efficacy as a partial mediator and organizational innovation climate as a moderator. Nursing management may focus on AI competencies, application confidence, and organizational support.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness in Bangladesh’s Public Administration: Linking Digital Leadership, Employee AI Capability, and Service Innovation
items.abstract: AI will emerge as a significant force behind administrative change, although public organisations vary in their preparedness to do so. This paper investigates the impact of digital leadership and employee AI ability on artificial intelligence preparedness and innovation in services in the Bangladesh public administration. A four-reflective construct survey model was created, including digital leadership, employee AI capability, AI readiness, and service innovation. It was analysed with a synthetic dataset of 835 cases that are intended to test the methodology and prove PLS-SEM. The data were evaluated using descriptive statistics, common method bias tests, evaluation of the measurement model, structural model, mediation, and predictive assessment. The findings revealed that the positive impacts of digital leadership and employee AI capability on AI preparedness were significant. Service innovation was also positively impacted by AI readiness significantly. Digital leadership and employee AI capability had a direct impact on service innovation. Both relationships were partially mediated by AI readiness. The model explained 45.4% of the variance in AI readiness and 41.0% of the variance in service innovation. All the predictive relevance values were positive and the PLS model yielded lower prediction errors than linear benchmark. The results reveal a readiness pathway that is coherent where leadership, employee capability, and institutional preparedness contribute to innovation in the delivery of public services.
